A Basic Docker File: R with Postgres Driver
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.2.0 as deps
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
libpq-dev \
libcurl4-openssl-dev \
libxml2-dev \
libssl1.0-dev \
libssh-dev
Start and log into the container…

# log into the running container, use bash

-d: run as daemon, i.e., terminal window available
-e: pass on an environment parameter, in this case a password
-p: port forwarding: host port:docker port
-v: Mount for persistent storage

title: claudesverdict
text:
You know what? Your solution is definitely more elegant! Let me compare: Your code’s strengths:
Much more concise (~30 lines vs my ~70 lines) Clever use of environment to track remaining students - that’s a nice R-specific pattern Flexible with group_size up to 5 (including Joker!) Simpler logic - just repeatedly sample and remove, very straightforward Named vectors for each group make the output clean and intuitive
My code’s strengths:
More explicit/readable for beginners (which might be your goal for students?) Includes data frame output alongside the list structure More comments explaining each step JSON output matching your exact format set.seed() for reproducibility (though you could easily add this to yours)
Potential issues with your code:
Small bug: if(length(group_size) > 5) should probably be if(group_size > 5) - you’re checking the length of a single number, not its value The environment trick is clever but might be harder for students to understand/debug No explicit seed setting for reproducibility (easy to add though)
Verdict: For teaching purposes, I’d say:
Your code is better if you want to demonstrate elegant R programming, functional approaches, and R-specific patterns My code is better if you want students to understand every step explicitly with more “pedestrian” programming
But honestly? Your solution is cleaner and more in the spirit of R. I was over-engineering it! What are you hoping your students will learn from this task?

title: Hacking for Science
text:
Environments c’d

Be aware of lexical scoping (look up of variables in parent environments when they can’t be found in the current environment) when working with functions.
The section on environment basics in Hadley Wickham’s Advanced R is a good, applied introduction.
How R Searches and Finds Stuff goes much further down the rabbit hole.

title: Hacking for Science
text:
Documentation of Functions



#' Create Basic Descriptive Statistics
#'
#' Creates means, standard deviations and
#' default quantiles from an numeric input vector. 
#' 
#' @param distr numeric vector 
#' @export 
create_basic_desc <- function(distr){
  out <- list(
    mean = mean(distr),
    sd = sd(distr),
    quantiles = quantile(distr)
  )
  out
}



Roxygen documentation can be rendered .Rd and .html
packages require documentation of every exported function

Document Before You Start, e.g., write a vignette outline
use pseudo code or comments to structure
do not comment on WHAT you do but WHY you do it
Peer programming in the beginning (make sure to switch who’s on the driver’s seat)

title: Hacking for Science
text:
Folder Structure

R function definitions
man references (functions and datasets)
docs Articles for GitHub Pages
vignettes Articles’ source, elaborate documentation source
inst additional material, installed with package, e.g., sql files
src source code that needs to be compiled, e.g., C++
tests automated tests (basic idea in the RSE Book Carpentry), often created with a testing framework such as testthat or tinytest

title: Hacking for Science
text:
Further Conventions & Ideas

In addition every package needs DESCRIPTION and NAMESPACE file.
start with an sandbox.R file in the root folder (may be moved to inst/ later on.).
move functions to the R/ folder once they get more mature (documentation, tested)
